qt: to the Commission Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Séverine Werbrouck (PfE), Jorge Martín Frías (PfE), António Tânger Corrêa (PfE), Mireia Borrás Pabón (PfE) Subject:

Agricultural trade between the EU and Morocco is governed by the EU-Morocco Association Agreement, expanded in 2012 to further liberalise agricultural trade. During the 2024/2025 season, Morocco exported around 570 000 tonnes of tomatoes to the EU, representing 70 % of EU imports from third countries, up 8 % over a year. This competition is expected to intensify further: in Dakhla, a new plot of 5 200 hectares, irrigated by desalinated sea water, is set to be primarily used to grow vegetables, in particular tomatoes, mostly for export. This model raises serious environmental concerns, owing to the desalination process and transport to Europe in particular, as well as social concerns, because of the working conditions and differences in labour costs. For years, however, the worries of European producer organisations about this unfair competition have fallen on deaf ears in the Commission. When will the Commission finally react and take real measures to protect European producers from this competition, which is destroying their industries and jobs? Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) The Commission follows closely market developments, including on imports of agricultural products. The EU tomato market remains mainly an intra-EU supplied market. Tomato imports from Morocco in the first nine months of 2026 amounted to 344,140 tonnes or 4.4% less than in the same period in 2025. Competition from tomatoes exported from Morocco is particularly present in the winter season. The Commission remains vigilant in monitoring and the proper implementation of the EUMorocco Association Agreement. Overall, this Agreement has been beneficial for EU exports to Morocco in many sectors, including the agri-food sector taken as a whole. Since 2022, the EU has enjoyed an overall trade surplus in agricultural products. In case of evidence of market disturbances, the Commission may use various measures according to the applicable legislation, including trade defence action if necessary. Member States have a broad array of interventions available to support the fruit and vegetables sector through the Common Agricultural Policy strategic plans, especially through operational programmes run by producer organisations that include measures aimed at improving production planning, boosting the commercial value of produce and promoting quality which contribute to a more competitive and market oriented sector. The Commission recognises the growing importance of ensuring high global standards and announced in the Vision for Agriculture and Food1 a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, in line with international rules. The EU shares some environmental challenges with Morocco and continues to address them through its EU-Morocco Green Partnership.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and
Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions A Vision for Agriculture and Food Shaping together an attractive farming and agri-food sector for future generations (COM/2025/75 final).
